blocks.text: Picture a spreadsheet of daily stock prices sitting in front of you. Someone asks what changed from yesterday to today. Your first instinct is to look at today's row and yesterday's row at the same time and do the subtraction. That instinct, lining up 'today's value' next to 'yesterday's value' in the same row, is exactly what pandas .shift() exists to automate. It takes a column and slides its values forward or backward relative to where they started, without touching the row labels sitting next to them. Once the mechanic clicks, a huge chunk of time series work, day over day change, week over week growth, predicting tomorrow from today, starts to feel almost mechanical.

blocks.alt: A diagram showing shift with positive periods moving values down toward later rows and shift with negative periods moving values up toward earlier rows
blocks.caption: The sign of the periods argument decides which direction values travel.

blocks.text: 1. Introduction

Here is the plain English version of what shift does. It takes every value in a column and slides it up or down by however many rows you tell it to, while the index stays exactly where it is. Nothing about the row labels changes. Only the values move. That one sentence explains almost everything you will do with shift for the rest of this lesson.

You will run into this constantly in time series work. Any time someone mentions 'yesterday's value', 'last week's total', or a model that 'looks back one step', there is a good chance shift is doing the heavy lifting behind the scenes. It is a small method, but it is one of the most quietly load bearing tools in the entire pandas time series toolkit.

blocks.text: 2. The Core Mechanic of shift

Strip away everything else and shift does one thing: it moves the values in a column a fixed number of rows in one direction, either down toward later rows or up toward earlier rows. That fixed number of rows is called periods, and it defaults to 1. Everything else in this lesson is really just this one idea applied to different problems.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({'value': [10, 20, 30, 40]})
df['shifted'] = df['value'].shift(1)
print(df)

blocks.text: 2.1 Moving Values Down with shift(1)

Call shift(1) and every value moves down one row. Whatever used to be in row 2 now shows up in row 3. Whatever used to be in row 1 now shows up in row 2. And row 1 itself? There is no row before it to pull a value from, so pandas has nothing to put there except NaN. That first NaN is not a bug, it is pandas being honest that no earlier value exists.

code.content:
df = pd.DataFrame({'value': [10, 20, 30]})
df['prev'] = df['value'].shift(1)
print(df)
#    value  prev
# 0     10   NaN
# 1     20  10.0
# 2     30  20.0

blocks.alt: A diagram showing shift of one moving row values down by one position, with the first row becoming NaN since there is no row before it
blocks.caption: shift(1): each row now holds what the previous row used to hold, and row 1 has nothing to inherit.

blocks.title: Read it as "the previous row's value"
blocks.content: Whenever you see .shift(1), read it in your head as 'give me what the row above used to have'. That mental translation makes almost every use of shift in this lesson easier to follow.

blocks.text: 2.2 Moving Values Up with shift(-1)

shift(-1) is the mirror image. Instead of pulling from the row above, it pulls from the row below. Every value moves up one row, so each row now shows what the next row used to hold. The very last row has no row after it to pull from, so it becomes NaN instead.

code.content:
df = pd.DataFrame({'value': [10, 20, 30]})
df['next'] = df['value'].shift(-1)
print(df)
#    value  next
# 0     10  20.0
# 1     20  30.0
# 2     30   NaN

blocks.alt: A diagram showing shift of negative one moving row values up by one position, with the last row becoming NaN since there is no row after it
blocks.caption: shift(-1): each row now holds what the next row used to hold, and the last row has nothing to inherit.

blocks.text: 2.3 The Index Never Moves

This is the detail people miss the first time they use shift. The index, the row labels themselves, do not move at all. Row 0 is still called row 0 after you shift. Only the values sitting inside that row change. If your DataFrame is indexed by date, the dates stay exactly where they are, it is only the numbers next to them that slide.

blocks.alt: A diagram showing that the index labels stay fixed in place while only the underlying values slide down one row
blocks.caption: Default shift repositions values within the existing rows. The row labels themselves are untouched.

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.content: Because the index does not move, a shifted column always lines up perfectly with the original column, row for row. That alignment is exactly what makes subtracting one from the other, which is the next section, so straightforward.

blocks.text: 3. Computing Period over Period Change

The single most common thing people actually use shift for is computing how much something changed from one period to the next. Because a shifted column lines up row for row with the original, subtracting the two gives you the change directly, no manual looping, no matching dates by hand.
3.1 Subtracting a Shifted Column

If df['price'] holds today's price in every row, then df['price'].shift(1) holds yesterday's price in every row, already lined up correctly. Subtract one from the other and you get the day over day change in a single line.

code.content:
df['change'] = df['price'] - df['price'].shift(1)
print(df)
#     price  change
# 0     100     NaN
# 1     105     5.0
# 2     103    -2.0

blocks.alt: A diagram showing today price minus a shifted previous price column producing the period over period change
blocks.caption: The original column minus its own shift(1) gives the day over day change, row by row.

blocks.text: 3.2 pct_change as the Built In Shortcut

Change in absolute terms is useful, but percent change is usually what people actually want to compare across different price levels. You can compute it by hand with the same shift trick: subtract the shifted value, then divide by the shifted value. Or you can skip the manual formula entirely and call pct_change(), which does exactly this division for you in one call.

code.content:
# manual version, using shift directly
df['pct_manual'] = (df['price'] - df['price'].shift(1)) / df['price'].shift(1)

# built in shortcut, same result
df['pct_change'] = df['price'].pct_change()

blocks.alt: A diagram showing a manual formula built from a shifted column and the pct_change built in method both arriving at the same percent change result
blocks.caption: pct_change() is not a different idea, it is the same shift based division wrapped in one convenient call.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Code","What It Computes"],"rows":[["Manual formula","(df['price'] - df['price'].shift(1)) / df['price'].shift(1)","Percent change, built by hand out of shift and subtraction"],["Built in shortcut","df['price'].pct_change()","The identical percent change, in a single call"]]}

blocks.text: 4. A Shifted Column as a Predictive Feature

Change and percent change are both about describing the past. But shift has a second, arguably even more important job: producing an input feature for a model. A model that is trying to predict tomorrow's price often benefits enormously from literally being shown yesterday's actual price as one of its inputs. That is exactly what shift(1) hands you.

code.content:
df['price_prev'] = df['price'].shift(1)

# a model could now take price_prev as an input feature
# when trying to predict today's price
features = df[['price_prev']]
target = df['price']

blocks.alt: A diagram showing yesterday actual price feeding into a model as an input feature that produces a predicted tomorrow price
blocks.caption: A shifted column handed to a model as an input is the seed of what a lag feature actually is.

blocks.title: This is a preview, not the full picture
blocks.content: Turning shifted columns into a systematic set of model inputs, deciding how many periods back to go, which columns are worth lagging, how to name them, is its own dedicated topic. The Lag Features lesson coming up next in this course builds directly on the mechanic you just learned here, so keep this example in mind. For now, the only thing to take away is that a lag feature is fundamentally just a shifted column.

blocks.text: 5. Row Based Shift vs Time Based Shift with freq

Everything so far has been what you could call row based shifting: values move to a different row position, and the index just comes along unchanged. But shift() has another mode entirely, triggered by the freq parameter, and it is important not to confuse the two.
5.1 The Default: Shifting by Row Position

Without freq, shift(1) counts rows. It does not care what the index actually contains, dates, integers, strings, it just moves values down by one physical row. This is the behavior you have seen in every example so far.

code.content:
df = pd.DataFrame(
    {'price': [100, 105, 103]},
    index=pd.to_datetime(['2024-01-01', '2024-01-02', '2024-01-03'])
)
print(df['price'].shift(1))
# 2024-01-01      NaN
# 2024-01-02    100.0
# 2024-01-03    105.0
# dates are unchanged, only the values moved

blocks.text: 5.2 Shifting by Real Time with freq

Pass freq='1D' and the operation changes completely. Instead of repositioning values within the existing rows, shift now moves the date index itself forward by a real calendar amount. Every timestamp in the index gets pushed forward by one day, and the values stay matched to their original row. Nothing gets left behind as NaN, because nothing is being pulled from a row that does not exist, the dates themselves are simply relabeled.

code.content:
shifted_index = df['price'].shift(1, freq='1D')
print(shifted_index)
# 2024-01-02    100
# 2024-01-03    105
# 2024-01-04    103
# same values, but every date moved forward by one day

blocks.alt: A diagram contrasting default row based shift, which moves values while the index stays put, with freq based shift, which moves the date index itself forward
blocks.caption: Two genuinely different operations that both happen to be called shift. Do not mix them up.

blocks.title: freq needs a real DatetimeIndex
blocks.content: This only works if your DataFrame or Series is actually indexed by dates. Try freq on a plain integer index and pandas has no calendar to shift along, so it will raise an error.

blocks.text: 6. The NaN Gotcha at the Boundaries
Every row based shift you do is going to leave at least one NaN behind, and it is worth being deliberate about what happens next instead of letting it slide through unnoticed.
6.1 Why the NaN Shows Up

shift(1) pulls each value from the row before it. The first row has no row before it, so there is nothing to pull, and pandas fills that gap with NaN. shift(-1) has the exact same problem at the opposite end: the last row has no row after it, so it becomes NaN instead. This is not something you can configure away, it is a direct, unavoidable consequence of shifting values past the edge of your data.

blocks.alt: A diagram showing a shifted column with a NaN at the boundary flowing into a decision point that branches into dropping the row or filling it
blocks.caption: A shift always produces a NaN at one boundary. What you do about it is a decision you have to make.

blocks.text: 6.2 Handling It Deliberately

Leaving that NaN sitting in your data unaddressed is asking for trouble later, especially once you start feeding shifted columns into calculations or into a model. This connects directly back to the Handling Missing Values lesson: the same two tools apply here, dropna and fillna, you just now have a very specific, very predictable reason for why the NaN exists.

code.content:
df['prev'] = df['price'].shift(1)

# option 1: drop the row that has no valid previous value
df_clean = df.dropna(subset=['prev'])

# option 2: fill it with something explicit instead of leaving it blank
df['prev_filled'] = df['prev'].fillna(0)

blocks.title: Watch for NaN chaining downstream
blocks.content: If you compute df['change'] using a shifted column that already has a NaN in it, that NaN carries straight through into change as well. Decide on a handling strategy before you build more calculations on top of the shifted column, not after.

Let's put shift(1) and pct_change() to work together on one continuous example: a small stock price dataset, computing the previous day's price, the day over day change, and the day over day percent change, all in the same DataFrame.

blocks.caption: Day 2's previous price is day 1's price. Day 3's previous price is day 2's price. That is the whole mechanic.

With prev_price sitting right there, the change column is just a subtraction.

blocks.text: 8. Summary and What Comes Next

shift() is a small method carrying a lot of weight. Once you can see it clearly, a lot of pandas time series code stops looking like magic and starts looking like a handful of the same trick applied in different places.

items: shift(1) moves values down one row, the first row becomes NaN
shift(-1) moves values up one row, the last row becomes NaN
the index itself never moves under the default row based shift, only the values do
subtracting a shifted column from the original gives period over period change, and pct_change() gives the percent version in one call
a shifted column handed to a model as an input is the seed of a lag feature
freq='1D' is a genuinely different operation, it moves the date index itself rather than repositioning values
the NaN a shift leaves behind needs a deliberate answer, dropna or fillna, not silence
